case_study_insert.main_stem: Kalder Timber Products (KTP) is a public limited company in the sustainable forestry and timber-board sector, employing a workforce of 73. Founded in 1998 by Elowen Kalder, it supplies graded board to furniture makers and operates a hierarchical structure with formal downward communication. KTP plans to invest $640,000 in a biomass-powered kiln-drying line, financed by a $250,000 bank loan and $390,000 from the sale of surplus land. It has fixed costs of $330,000 a year, a variable cost of $14.00 a unit and a selling price of $25.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. KTP faces a board-grading defect rate of 3.8% and rising labour turnover among kiln operators, which Elowen wants addressed.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Production Report — Q3 2025: The plant graded 11,250 boards last quarter with a defect rate of 3.8%, up from 2.4% a year ago. Customer quality complaints rose from 21 to 38 per month, and average order lead time is 5.2 days. Biomass drying trials cut kiln fuel use by 3.6% but raised drying time by 0.8 days per batch. A survey of 320 furniture manufacturers found that 59% would pay up to $0.45 more for sustainably sourced, accurately graded board and 51% check forest certification before ordering. A skills audit shows 20 of 73 staff lack certification on the new kilns; accredited external courses cost $810 per operator.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans such as KTP's $250,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.60 to $13.41 per hour from April 2026, lifting wage bills in timber processing. (3) Resin, transport and fuel input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year, while housing completions grew 5.2% and furniture retail sales rose 2.9%.

questions.question_text: KTP plans to fund part of its $640,000 kiln line with a $250,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for KTP of using $390,000 from the sale of surplus land instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling surplus land raises $390,000 without interest or repayment obligations, so KTP avoids enlarging the $250,000 bank loan and protects cash flow while carrying $330,000 fixed costs and a 3.8% defect rate. Interest saved can be spent on grading checks, protecting the $25.00 selling price and the 45,000-unit output needed to justify the $640,000 biomass kiln.

Point 2: Using asset sales reduces the company's debt and the risk that lenders impose conditions or call in loans if cash generation slips, which is valuable for a public limited company accountable to shareholders. It also converts an idle asset into a productive one without dilution. Given rising labour turnover among kiln operators, the lower fixed-commitment burden gives Elowen Kalder more flexibility to invest in training and stability rather than meeting larger loan instalments.

A further point is that the $390,000 asset sale is a one-off: once the land is sold it cannot fund a second phase, whereas a loan could be drawn as needed. Elowen should ensure the proceeds cover the $640,000 project alongside the $250,000 loan, leaving reserves for the 20 kiln certifications at $810 each and the 3.8% defect clean-up, rather than tying up all cash in one project.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of asset sale over a larger loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to KTP's kiln line, existing loan and defect problem.

questions.question_text: KTP is launching sustainably sourced graded board. Consider furniture-trade exhibitions, regional press advertising, or direct account management with furniture makers. Which should KTP choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Furniture-trade exhibitions: Stand space at trade fairs would expose KTP's board to the 320 surveyed manufacturers and many specifiers, allowing samples and certification to be shown in person and supporting the premium that 59% will pay. The limitation is high cost for a $640,000 investment and a 73-employee firm, plus a narrow audience concentrated in a few venues.

Regional press advertising: Newspaper and trade supplements are relatively cheap and can repeatedly reach local furniture makers, building awareness of the sustainably sourced range. They suit a regional supplier. However, print cannot demonstrate grading accuracy or the 3.6% fuel saving, and it will not persuade the 51% of buyers who check forest certification, since adverts offer little evidence.

Direct account management: Assigning staff to manage key furniture-maker accounts lets KTP present certification, explain why the 3.8% defect rate is being cut and agree tailored grades. It builds long-term relationships and directly targets the 59% who will pay up to $0.45 more. It is slower to reach new customers and consumes staff time while labour turnover is rising.

Recommendation: KTP should choose direct account management, backed by a modest exhibition presence. Direct management converts the 59% willing to pay a premium and supplies the proof that 51% of buyers require. Exhibitions are rejected as expensive and narrow; regional press is rejected because it lacks the technical evidence that certification-focused furniture makers demand.

KTP should also recognise that the 51% of buyers who check forest certification are likely to be the same large accounts demanding consistent grading, so promotion must be backed by the quality programme that cuts the 3.8% defect rate; without it the $0.45 premium will not be sustained and the $640,000 kiln will not earn its return.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited reference to KTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KTP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discusses all three options in context with a justified recommendation explaining why exhibitions and press advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: KTP's defect rate is 3.8% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for KTP of using its hierarchical structure with formal downward communication to address these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A hierarchical structure gives KTP a clear chain of command from Elowen to the kiln floor, so a single grading standard can be issued to cut the 3.8% defect rate. Formal downward communication ensures every operator receives the same instructions about board grading, reducing the inconsistency behind 38 monthly complaints and protecting the $25.00 selling price and 45,000-unit output.

Point 2: Defined roles and formal directives let managers respond decisively when labour turnover creates vacancies, reallocating tasks so the $640,000 biomass kiln keeps running. Clear written procedures also shorten induction for new kiln operators, limiting the quality damage from inexperience. With fixed costs of $330,000 a year, this top-down control protects both output and the sustainable-forestry reputation that underpins the certified board range.

The limitation is that formal downward communication can suppress the operator feedback needed to diagnose the 3.8% grading defects, so Elowen should create an upward channel as well. With 20 of 73 staff needing kiln certification and turnover rising, a rigid hierarchy may lose the very skills the $640,000 line depends on.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of hierarchical/formal structures (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to KTP's 3.8% defects, turnover and kiln investment.

questions.question_text: KTP must certify 20 kiln operators. Consider accredited external courses at $810 per operator or on-the-job coaching. Which should KTP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Accredited external courses at $810 per operator: Formal certification gives the 20 operators a recognised standard of kiln competence, which is valuable when the defect rate has risen to 3.8% and furniture makers check forest certification. The direct fee is $810 x 20 = $16,200, small beside the $640,000 investment. The drawbacks are time away from the kilns, short-term output loss and generic content that may not cover KTP's exact drying regime.

On-the-job coaching: Coaching at the kilns is specific to KTP's biomass equipment, costs no fees and keeps all 20 operators productive, protecting output of 45,000 boards. Experienced staff can demonstrate the fuel-saving routine from the 3.6% trial. However, bad habits can spread, there is no external certificate, and with labour turnover rising the benefit may be lost when trained staff leave.

Decision: KTP should choose accredited external courses followed by on-site coaching. The certificate helps reverse the rise from 2.4% to 3.8% defects and reassures the 51% of buyers checking certification, and $16,200 is modest against $640,000. On-the-job coaching alone is rejected because it offers no recognised proof of competence and is undermined by rising labour turnover.

KTP should also consider the 5.2-day lead time: releasing 20 operators for $810 courses could delay orders and aggravate the 38 monthly complaints, so training should be staggered. Yet with the defect rate up from 2.4% to 3.8%, external certification is the more reliable route to consistent grading for the 59% of buyers paying a premium, and the $16,200 cost is trivial against $640,000.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of KTP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, certification and turnover, rejecting the alternative.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KTP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $11.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety against 45,000-unit output; premium pricing for the $0.45 certified board; investment cover for the $640,000 kiln; and unit-cost benchmarking at $21.33 to attack defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $330,000 / ($25.00 - $14.00) = $330,000 / $11.00 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $25.00 - $14.00 = $11.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $11.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KTP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 30,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 45,000 units gives a margin of safety of 15,000 units, showing the demand fall the $640,000 kiln can withstand.
2. Contribution of $11.00 lets managers quantify the $0.45 premium that 59% of furniture makers accept: at $25.45 contribution becomes $11.45, supporting certification spending.
3. With $330,000 fixed costs and $11.00 contribution, managers can set the volume needed to service the $250,000 bank loan from the kiln investment.
4. Average total cost of $330,000 / 45,000 + $14.00 is about $21.33 a unit; tracking it exposes the extra cost of the 3.8% defect rate and longer drying time.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KTP's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has KTP's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 24.0%
ROCE 2025 = 30.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit of $1,800,000 on revenue of $4,000,000 gives 45.0% in 2024; $2,500,000 on $5,000,000 gives 50.0% in 2025. Operating profit of $600,000 on $4,000,000 revenue is 15.0%, and $900,000 on $5,000,000 is 18.0% in 2025. Returns on the capital base are $600,000 / $2,500,000 = 24.0% and $900,000 / $3,000,000 = 30.0%.

Evaluation: Every measure improved. The gross margin rose from 45.0% to 50.0%, so cost of sales absorbed less of the $5,000,000 revenue, helped by the 3.6% kiln-fuel saving. Operating margin improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, meaning operating profit grew faster than revenue despite the 3.8% defect problem. The return on capital increased from 24.0% to 30.0%, so the extra $500,000 of capital employed is being used more productively. ROCE is the strongest evidence here because it links the $900,000 operating profit to the $3,000,000 capital base, showing that the $640,000 biomass investment is already earning returns; the gross margin alone could rise merely from lower timber input prices. Capital employed grew, so the higher return is not an artefact of a shrinking asset base. Interest payable rose from $45,000 to $60,000, a modest increase that does not explain the profit growth.

Conclusion: KTP's financial performance has improved. All three measures moved in the same favourable direction and the gains are driven by stronger profit, not accounting effects.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three profitability measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of margins and capital use and a justified conclusion, naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KTP of using biomass energy in its kiln-drying line.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Biomass trials cut kiln fuel use by 3.6%, lowering the $14.00 variable cost per unit and protecting the $11.00 contribution. It also reinforces the sustainably sourced proposition that 59% of surveyed furniture makers will pay up to $0.45 more for and that 51% check through forest certification, supporting the $640,000 kiln and output of 45,000 graded boards.

Disadvantage: Biomass plant requires capital and reliable fuel supply, adding to the $330,000 fixed costs; a fuel shortage could halt drying and worsen the 3.8% defect rate. Trials also raised drying time by 0.8 days per batch, which slows order fulfilment against a 5.2-day lead time. With 20 of 73 staff uncertified and labour turnover rising, operating the new system safely adds training pressure.

Elowen should set the 3.6% fuel saving against the 0.8-day longer drying time and the 5.2-day lead time, since slower kilns could worsen the 38 monthly complaints. The $810 certification for 20 operators is also needed before the $640,000 biomass line can be run reliably.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to KTP's trial data, survey and costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in resin, transport and fuel input costs will affect KTP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): The increase is 0.75 percentage points. If KTP's $250,000 expansion loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $250,000 = $1,875, small relative to $330,000 fixed costs. A fixed-rate loan removes the immediate cash effect, though future borrowing may cost more and higher rates could slow housing completions, a source of demand for furniture and board.

Minimum wage rise (6.4%, to $13.41 per hour): KTP employs a workforce of 73 in grading and kiln roles largely paid hourly, so wage costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so an annual wage total cannot be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 45,000 units / 73 staff, about 616 boards per worker. If that holds, the rise is manageable; if rising labour turnover reduces it, unit labour cost climbs and the $11.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (10.8% on resin, transport and fuel): The insert does not decompose the $14.00 variable cost, so only a bounded calculation is shown: if the whole variable cost rose 10.8%, that adds 10.8% x $14.00 = $1.512, about $1.51 a unit; across 45,000 units that is about $68,040 a year. Contribution would fall from $11.00 toward $9.49.

Conclusion: The 10.8% input-cost rise has the greatest impact. It applies to every board graded, directly erodes the $11.00 contribution that funds the $640,000 kiln and cannot be removed by fixing a loan. The interest rise is at most $1,875 and the wage rise can be offset by productivity; neither affects every unit.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to KTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KTP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three changes with shown derivations from insert figures and a justified greatest-impact judgement rejecting the other two.
